claim: Artemisinin-based therapies are the only effective treatment for malaria.
source: Artemisinin-based therapies are the only effective treatment for malaria, the most devastating disease in human history.
evidence: Supported by citation to Okell et al., 2014 in the Introduction section

claim: The demand for ACTs reached nearly 400 million treatment courses in 2013.
source: there is a steadily increasing demand for ACTs which reached nearly 400 million treatment courses in 2013 (http://www.who.int/malaria/publications/world_malaria_report_2014)
evidence: Supported by reference to WHO malaria report

claim: The reactive endoperoxide bridge in artemisinin is believed to be responsible for its medicinal properties.
source: The mechanism of action of artemisinin on the malaria parasites Plasmodium falciparium and P. vivax is not entirely clear, but it is generally believed that the reactive endoperoxide bridge present in the molecule (Figure 1) is responsible for its medicinal properties.
evidence: Stated as general belief in the field, with reference to Figure 1 showing the molecular structure

claim: Artemisinin and its derivatives are considered as promising anti-cancer, antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents.
source: In addition to their antimalarial activity, artemisinin and its derivatives are currently also considered as promising anti-cancer, antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents (e.g., Willoughby et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Willoughby et al., 2009

claim: In A. annua, artemisinin is produced in the cytosol of the glandular trichomes of leaves and flowers.
source: In A. annua, artemisinin is produced in the cytosol of the glandular trichomes of leaves and flowers (Tang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2014

claim: Amorphadiene synthase (ADS) catalyzes the first committed step of the artemisinin biosynthesis pathway.
source: The biosynthesis initiates with the conversion of the isoprenoid building blocks IPP and DMAPP into farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) which is then converted into amorpha-4,11-diene by amorphadiene synthase (ADS), the enzyme catalyzing the first committed step of the pathway (Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 1 showing the pathway

claim: Amorpha-4,11-diene is a volatile compound.
source: Amorpha-4,11-diene is a volatile compound that is oxidized to artemisinic alcohol and subsequently to artemisinic aldehyde by the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase CYP71AV1 (CYP) and its redox partner, the cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR).
evidence: Stated as a property of the compound in the pathway description

claim: Artemisinic acid can be efficiently and cheaply converted to artemisinin by chemical means.
source: Artemisinic acid can be efficiently and cheaply converted to artemisinin by chemical means (Paddon et al., 2013; Kopetzki et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Paddon et al., 2013 and Kopetzki et al., 2013

claim: Artemisinic acid represents a high-value precursor for the industrial production of artemisinin-based pharmaceuticals.
source: Artemisinic acid can be efficiently and cheaply converted to artemisinin by chemical means (Paddon et al., 2013; Kopetzki et al., 2013) and, therefore, represents a high-value precursor for the industrial production of artemisinin-based pharmaceuticals (Paddon and Keasling, 2014).
evidence: Stated as inference from chemical conversion efficiency, supported by citations

claim: Semisynthetic synthesis in yeast represents the most efficient heterologous production system for artemisinic acid.
source: Currently, the semisynthetic synthesis in yeast (Paddon et al., 2013) represents the most efficient heterologous production system for artemisinic acid, the immediate precursor of artemisinin (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paddon et al., 2013

claim: The production costs of artemisinic acid in yeast are still high.
source: However, the production costs are still high and ACTs remain unaffordable to many people in the tropical and subtropical regions of Africa and Asia that are most severely afflicted with malaria.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of current yeast-based production

claim: Production in yeast requires large volumes of costly synthetic culture media and large-capacity bioreactors run under sterile conditions.
source: Since production in yeast requires large volumes of costly synthetic culture media and large-capacity bioreactors run under sterile conditions, production in plants can potentially provide a much cheaper, renewable and easily scalable source of artemisinic acid.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of yeast-based production systems

claim: Production of artemisinic compounds at low levels has been shown to be feasible in heterologous plant systems.
source: Although the production of artemisinic compounds at low levels has been shown to be feasible in heterologous plant systems (Wu et al., 2006; van Herpen et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2011; Farhi et al., 2011), the development of an efficient production system for the drug precursor artemisinic acid has not been achieved.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: The development of an efficient production system for artemisinic acid in plants has not been achieved prior to this work.
source: Although the production of artemisinic compounds at low levels has been shown to be feasible in heterologous plant systems (Wu et al., 2006; van Herpen et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2011; Farhi et al., 2011), the development of an efficient production system for the drug precursor artemisinic acid has not been achieved.
evidence: Stated as a gap in the field that this work addresses

claim: The core enzymes to synthesize artemisinic acid are FPS, ADS, CYP and CPR.
source: The core enzymes to synthesize artemisinic acid are FPS, ADS, CYP and CPR (Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in Results section with reference to pathway diagram

claim: Four synthetic artemisinic acid operon constructs (pAO1-4) were built and introduced into the chloroplast genome of tobacco plants.
source: Four synthetic artemisinic acid operon constructs (pAO1-4) were built and introduced into the chloroplast (plastid) genome of tobacco plants by particle gun-mediated transformation.
evidence: Described as experimental procedure performed in this study

claim: Transplastomic lines were selected on regeneration medium with spectinomycin and purified to homoplasmy.
source: Chloroplast-transformed (transplastomic) lines were selected on regeneration medium with spectinomycin and purified to homoplasmy by additional rounds of selection and regeneration (Svab and Maliga, 1993; Bock, 2015).
evidence: Described as experimental procedure with supporting citations

claim: RFLP analysis verified integration of the synthetic operon constructs into the plastid genome by homologous recombination.
source: Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis verified integration of the synthetic operon constructs into the plastid genome by homologous recombination and successful elimination of all wild-type copies of the highly polyploid chloroplast genome (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2B

claim: Homoplasmy of the transplastomic lines was verified by seed assays that confirmed lack of segregation of the spectinomycin resistance and uniparentally maternal inheritance.
source: Homoplasmy of the transplastomic lines was additionally verified by seed assays that confirmed lack of segregation of the spectinomycin resistance and uniparentally maternal inheritance (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2C

claim: All homoplasmic transplastomic lines grew autotrophically under greenhouse conditions and produced viable seeds.
source: All homoplasmic transplastomic lines grew autotrophically under greenhouse conditions and produced viable seeds.
evidence: Observed phenotype of the generated plants

claim: Transplastomic lines obtained with constructs pAO1 and pAO3 displayed a slightly pale-green phenotype and a subtle growth delay at the juvenile stage.
source: However, transplastomic lines obtained with constructs pAO1 and pAO3 (Figure 2A) displayed a slightly pale-green phenotype and a subtle growth delay at the juvenile stage (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed phenotype shown in figures

claim: Chlorophylls and carotenoids are significantly reduced in plants exhibiting the mild phenotype.
source: Measurement of chlorophylls and carotenoids confirmed that, indeed, both pigment classes are significantly reduced in plants exhibiting the mild phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Experimental measurement shown in supplementary figures

claim: All transplastomic lines accumulated the volatile artemisinic acid precursor amorpha-4,11-diene and its first oxidation product artemisinic alcohol.
source: Metabolite profiling (see Materials and Methods) of the transplastomic lines revealed that all lines accumulated the volatile artemisinic acid precursor amorpha-4,11-diene and its first oxidation product artemisinic alcohol (Figure 1; Figure 3).
evidence: Metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 3

claim: Amorpha-4,11-diene accumulated to lower levels in the lines displaying the subtle phenotype.
source: Interestingly, amorpha-4,11-diene accumulated to lower levels in the lines displaying the subtle phenotype, whereas artemisinic alcohol was detected in similar amounts in all transplastomic plants.
evidence: Metabolite profiling comparison between lines

claim: Accumulation of artemisinic acid correlated with the altered phenotype in Nt-AO1-1 and Nt-AO3-1.
source: Accumulation of artemisinic acid correlated with the altered phenotype in Nt-AO1-1 and Nt-AO3-1, suggesting that a more efficient conversion of amorpha-4,11-diene to downstream metabolites could be the cause of the phenotype.
evidence: Correlation observed in metabolite profiling data

claim: In Nt-AO2 plants, artemisinic acid accumulates only in mature leaves of young and flowering plants.
source: These analyses also confirmed the inverse relationship between artemisinic acid and amorpha-4,11-diene accumulation (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Developmental analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: High artemisinic acid accumulation correlated with a high CYP/CPR expression ratio in Nt-AO3 plants.
source: When the expression of the four transgenes was assayed, a striking difference was observed in the CYP/CPR expression ratio in that high artemisinic acid accumulation correlated with a high CYP/CPR expression ratio in Nt-AO3 plants (Figure 4D–G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Northern blot and qRT-PCR analysis shown in figures

claim: CYPs are often found in excess to their CPR counterparts in nature, with ratios of 10–100:1 or higher.
source: In nature, CYPs are often found in excess to their CPR counterparts, with ratios of 10–100:1 or higher (reviewed, e.g., in Guengerich, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Guengerich, 2002

claim: CPRs can activate molecular oxygen, thereby producing superoxide radicals and wasting redox capacity of the cell.
source: Even though there is currently no consensus explanation for this observation, it is known that CPRs can activate molecular oxygen, thereby producing superoxide radicals and wasting redox capacity of the cell (Manoj et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manoj et al., 2010

claim: The levels of the CPR transcript and the CPR protein remain constant during development of A. annua and in different organs.
source: This explanation is also in agreement with published data on transcript accumulation and protein abundance for these two enzymes in A. annua. While the levels of the CPR transcript and the CPR protein remain constant during development of the plant and in different organs, the transcript and protein levels of CYP increase in the developmental stages and organs where artemisinin synthesis is induced (Olofsson et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Olofsson et al., 2011 and Zeng et al., 2008

claim: The transcript and protein levels of CYP increase in the developmental stages and organs where artemisinin synthesis is induced in A. annua.
source: While the levels of the CPR transcript and the CPR protein remain constant during development of the plant and in different organs, the transcript and protein levels of CYP increase in the developmental stages and organs where artemisinin synthesis is induced (Olofsson et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Olofsson et al., 2011 and Zeng et al., 2008

claim: The final oxidation step from artemisinic aldehyde to artemisinic acid requires an effective monooxygenase.
source: Especially the final oxidation step from artemisinic aldehyde to artemisinic acid appears to require an effective monooxygenase (Ting et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ting et al., 2013

claim: 612 kanamycin-resistant shoots (Nt-AO-CS lines) were generated by supertransformation of the transplastomic recipient lines Nt-AO2-1 and Nt-AO3-1.
source: 612 kanamycin-resistant shoots (Nt-AO-CS lines) were generated by supertransformation of the transplastomic recipient lines Nt-AO2-1 and Nt-AO3-1.
evidence: Experimental result from transformation procedure

claim: 199 COSTREL lines were selected for metabolic screening of artemisinic compounds: 79 Nt-AO2-CS and 120 Nt-AO3-CS lines.
source: Based on growth, phenotype and fertility of the plants, 199 COSTREL lines were selected for metabolic screening of artemisinic compounds: 79 Nt-AO2-CS and 120 Nt-AO3-CS lines (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental screening procedure described

claim: The various COSTREL lines displayed great variation with respect to the accumulation levels of artemisinic compounds.
source: The various lines displayed great variation with respect to the accumulation levels of the compounds assayed (amorpha-4,11-diene, artemisinic alcohol, dihydroartemisinic alcohol, dihydroartemisinic acid and artemisinic acid).
evidence: Observed variation in metabolite profiling data

claim: In combinatorial transformation, all transgenes that simultaneously enter the nucleus usually integrate into the same genomic locus and co-segregate into the next generation.
source: In combinatorial transformation, all transgenes that simultaneously enter the nucleus of the recipient cell usually integrate into the same genomic locus (most likely into a transient DNA double-strand break), and therefore co-segregate into the next generation (Naqvi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Naqvi et al., 2009

claim: Among Nt-AO2-CS lines, the highest increase in artemisinic acid content occurred in line 132 showing a 33-fold increase compared to its transplastomic recipient line Nt-AO2-1.
source: These analyses confirmed the results obtained with the T0 plants and revealed that, in the case of the Nt-AO2-CS lines, the highest increase in artemisinic acid content occurred in line 132 showing a 33-fold increase compared to its transplastomic recipient line Nt-AO2-1
evidence: Metabolite profiling data from T1 generation

claim: Among Nt-AO3-CS lines, line 180 reached a 77-fold increase in artemisinic acid compared to transplastomic line Nt-AO3-1.
source: whereas among the Nt-AO3-CS lines, line 180 reached an even 77-fold increase compared to transplastomic line Nt-AO3-1 (Figure 5—source data 1; Figure 5A).
evidence: Metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The highest producer, line Nt-AO3-CS180, reached levels of 120.4 ± 42 mg artemisinic acid per kg FW in the T1 generation.
source: The trait artemisinic acid content was stable across generations, and the highest producer, line Nt-AO3-CS180, reached levels of 120.4 ± 42 mg per kg FW in the T1 generation.
evidence: Quantitative metabolite measurement data

claim: Increased amounts of artemisinic acid in the Nt-AO-CS lines were negatively correlated with the accumulation of artemisinic alcohol.
source: Increased amounts of artemisinic acid in the Nt-AO-CS lines were negatively correlated with the accumulation of artemisinic alcohol (Figure 5A,B), indicating that the efficiency of oxidation of the alcohol represents a key bottleneck in the pathway that we alleviated by supertransformation with the additional pathway genes.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: Artemisinic alcohol was reduced to nearly undetectable levels in the best-performing line Nt-AO3-CS180.
source: Importantly, artemisinic alcohol was reduced to nearly undetectable levels in the best-performing line Nt-AO3-CS180 suggesting that maximum conversion efficiency has been achieved (Figure 5B; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Metabolite profiling data shown in figures

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between amorpha-4,11-diene and artemisinic alcohol.
source: Another significant correlation at the metabolite level was a strong positive correlation between amorpha-4,11-diene and artemisinic alcohol (Tables 1 and 2)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis shown in Tables 1 and 2

claim: Amorpha-4,11-diene was not significantly correlated with artemisinic acid accumulation.
source: By contrast, amorpha-4,11-diene was not significantly correlated with artemisinic acid accumulation.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis

claim: Dihydroartemisinic acid was detected only in line Nt-AO3-CS180 in the T0 generation and in lines Nt-AO3-CS53 and Nt-AO3-CS180 in the T1 generation.
source: Dihydroartemisinic acid, the direct precursor of artemisinin, was detected only in line Nt-AO3-CS180 in the T0 generation and in lines Nt-AO3-CS53 and Nt-AO3-CS180 in the T1 generation (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 7C)
evidence: Metabolite profiling data shown in figures and source data

claim: Elevated artemisinic acid levels in Nt-AO3-CS lines were most strongly correlated with the presence of the ALDH1 transgene.
source: Statistical analysis revealed that elevated artemisinic acid levels in Nt-AO3-CS lines were most strongly correlated with the presence of the ALDH1 transgene.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of genotype-phenotype relationships

claim: The best-performing line (Nt-AO3-CS180) expresses dxr, ADH1, ALDH1 and DBR2 to high levels.
source: The results support the importance of dxr, ADH1, ALDH1 and DBR2 in boosting artemisinic acid synthesis and revealed that the best-performing line (Nt-AO3-CS180) expresses dxr, ADH1, ALDH1 and DBR2 to high levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: No significant phenotypic differences were observed between the best-performing COSTREL lines and their transplastomic recipient lines.
source: To test whether artemisinic acid accumulation is correlated with a visible phenotype of the plants, the best-performing COSTREL lines were compared with their transplastomic recipient lines. No significant phenotypic differences were observed and even line Nt-AO3-CS180 (that showed the strongest increase in artemisinic acid accumulation; Figure 5A) was nearly indistinguishable from its transplastomic recipient Nt-AO3-1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Visual comparison shown in Figure 5D

claim: Artemisinic acid is not toxic to plant cells.
source: This suggests that artemisinic acid is not toxic to plant cells (and that a further increase in artemisinic acid might be achievable).
evidence: Inferred from lack of phenotypic effects at high artemisinic acid levels

claim: There are no significant differences between transplastomic line Nt-AO3-1 and the best-performing COSTREL line Nt-AO3-CS180 in growth and biomass.
source: Growth and biomass measurements confirmed that there are no significant differences between transplastomic line Nt-AO3-1 and the best-performing COSTREL line Nt-AO3-CS180
evidence: Growth and biomass measurement data

claim: The COSTREL line showed only a small reduction in total leaf biomass (by on average 13%) compared to the wild type.
source: and revealed only a small reduction in total leaf biomass (by on average 13%) of the COSTREL line compared to the wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Biomass measurement data shown in supplementary figure

claim: None of the transplastomic lines and none of the analyzed COSTREL lines accumulated detectable levels of artemisinin.
source: None of our transplastomic lines and none of the analyzed COSTREL lines accumulated detectable levels of artemisinin (see Materials and Methods).
evidence: Metabolite profiling data

claim: Some of the best-performing COSTREL lines accumulated detectable amounts of dihydroartemisinic acid.
source: However, some of our best-performing COSTREL lines accumulated detectable amounts of dihydroartemisinic acid (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 7), the immediate precursor of artemisinin, indicating that DBR2 and ALDH1 can function in plastids.
evidence: Metabolite profiling data shown in figures

claim: DBR2 and ALDH1 can function in plastids.
source: However, some of our best-performing COSTREL lines accumulated detectable amounts of dihydroartemisinic acid (Figure 5—source data 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 7), the immediate precursor of artemisinin, indicating that DBR2 and ALDH1 can function in plastids.
evidence: Inferred from detection of dihydroartemisinic acid in plastid-engineered plants

claim: The chloroplast is likely to produce sufficient amounts of singlet oxygen to facilitate the spontaneous conversion of dihydroartemisinic acid into artemisinin.
source: The chloroplast is likely to produce sufficient amounts of singlet oxygen (which is a regular by-product of photosynthetic electron transfer) to facilitate the spontaneous conversion of dihydroartemisinic acid into artemisinin (Kopetzki et al., 2013; Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from known properties of chloroplasts and cited chemical conversion mechanism

claim: Artemisinin is highly toxic to photosynthetically active cells.
source: An alternative explanation for the lack of artemisinin accumulation could be that COSTREL lines that produce artemisinin were not recovered, because artemisinin is highly toxic to photosynthetically active cells (Bharati et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bharati et al., 2012

claim: For the foreseeable future, ACTs will remain the most powerful weapon in the world's battle against malaria.
source: For the foreseeable future, ACTs will remain the most powerful weapon in the world's battle against malaria (http://www.who.int/malaria/areas/treatment/overview/en/).
evidence: Supported by reference to WHO malaria treatment information

claim: When used as an oral monotherapy, artemisinin can promote the development of resistance in the malaria parasite.
source: When used as an oral monotherapy, artemisinin can promote the development of resistance in the parasite (Mok et al., 2015; Straimer et al., 2015; Mbengue et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mok et al., 2015; Straimer et al., 2015; Mbengue et al., 2015

claim: ACTs are based on fixed-dose co-formulations that combine two different active ingredients in one tablet.
source: and, therefore, ACTs are based on fixed-dose co-formulations that combine two different active ingredients in one tablet.
evidence: Stated as a consequence of resistance concerns

claim: A. annua produces artemisinin only in a very small fraction of the leaf cells (the glandular trichomes).
source: However, as A. annua produces artemisinin only in a very small fraction of the leaf cells (the glandular trichomes) and its cultivation is inefficient, slow and vulnerable to adverse environmental conditions, the development of a production method that is independent of A. annua is highly desirable (Bryant et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as a limitation of A. annua production with supporting citation

claim: Cultivation of A. annua is inefficient, slow and vulnerable to adverse environmental conditions.
source: However, as A. annua produces artemisinin only in a very small fraction of the leaf cells (the glandular trichomes) and its cultivation is inefficient, slow and vulnerable to adverse environmental conditions, the development of a production method that is independent of A. annua is highly desirable (Bryant et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as a limitation with supporting citation

claim: Tobacco is a high-biomass crop, grown in large acreages.
source: Tobacco is a high-biomass crop, grown in large acreages, for which alternative uses (that are unrelated to smoking) have long been sought.
evidence: Stated as a property of tobacco as a crop

claim: Tobacco is well suited for cultivation at high cropping densities and multiple harvests (4–5) per season are possible.
source: Since tobacco is well suited for cultivation at high cropping densities and multiple harvests (4–5) per season are possible, 40 t of biomass can be obtained from a single acre of tobacco field at a cost of only around $100 per ton
evidence: Stated as agricultural properties of tobacco with reference to production cost data

claim: 40 t of biomass can be obtained from a single acre of tobacco field at a cost of only around $100 per ton.
source: Since tobacco is well suited for cultivation at high cropping densities and multiple harvests (4–5) per season are possible, 40 t of biomass can be obtained from a single acre of tobacco field at a cost of only around $100 per ton (http://tobacco.ces.ncsu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/07/tobacco-production-cost-2011-1.pdf?fwd=no).
evidence: Supported by reference to tobacco production cost data

claim: With the best-performing COSTREL line, production levels of ~4.8 kg artemisinic acid per acre can be obtained.
source: Thus, with our best-performing COSTREL line, production levels of ~4.8 kg artemisinic acid per acre can be obtained
evidence: Calculated from biomass yield and artemisinic acid content data

claim: The current world demand for artemisinin is ~100 t.
source: suggesting that the current world demand (of ~100 t artemisinin) can be met by cultivating tobacco on an area of ~200 km2
evidence: Stated as current demand estimate

claim: The current world demand for artemisinin can be met by cultivating tobacco on an area of ~200 km2.
source: suggesting that the current world demand (of ~100 t artemisinin) can be met by cultivating tobacco on an area of ~200 km2, which is less than the area of the city of Boston (assuming ~50% loss during extraction and conversion of artemisinic acid to artemisinin; Paddon et al., 2013; Kopetzki et al., 2013).
evidence: Calculated from production levels with assumptions about conversion efficiency

claim: In A. annua the artemisinin biosynthetic pathway is confined to glandular trichomes.
source: Whereas in A. annua the artemisinin biosynthetic pathway is confined to glandular trichomes, our COSTREL tobacco lines produce artemisinic acid in chloroplasts and, thus, in the whole leaf.
evidence: Stated as a contrast to the engineered tobacco system

claim: The COSTREL tobacco lines produce artemisinic acid in chloroplasts and, thus, in the whole leaf.
source: Whereas in A. annua the artemisinin biosynthetic pathway is confined to glandular trichomes, our COSTREL tobacco lines produce artemisinic acid in chloroplasts and, thus, in the whole leaf.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the engineered system

claim: The redox environment in the cytosol of tobacco cells favors reduction of aldehydes to alcohols rather than their oxidation to acids.
source: Furthermore, previous transgenic work has shown that the redox environment in the cytosol of tobacco cells favors reduction of aldehydes to alcohols rather than their oxidation to acids, thus limiting the ability of the cytosolically located pathway to produce high quantities of artemisinic acid (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011

claim: The chloroplast offers a more favorable redox milieu that allows the quantitative conversion of artemisinic alcohol into artemisinic acid.
source: The high levels of artemisinic acid achieved in this work by implementing the pathway into plastids suggest that the chloroplast offers a more favorable redox milieu that allows the quantitative conversion of artemisinic alcohol into artemisinic acid (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Inferred from high artemisinic acid production in chloroplast-engineered plants

claim: Transgene expression from the plastid genome is generally very low in non-photosynthetic tissues and cell types.
source: This is because transgene expression from the plastid genome is generally very low in non-photosynthetic tissues and cell types.
evidence: Stated as a general property of plastid transformation

claim: Transgene expression in non-green tissues can be significantly enhanced by designing specific (chimeric) expression signals.
source: It can be significantly enhanced by designing specific (chimeric) expression signals that confer high transgene activity in non-green tissues (Zhang et al., 2012; Caroca et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2012 and Caroca et al., 2013

claim: The chloroplast represents an attractive site for engineering new metabolic pathways into plants.
source: The chloroplast represents an attractive site for engineering new metabolic pathways into plants.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the work

claim: The chloroplast contains large pools of diverse metabolites that can be tapped.
source: Being the biosynthetic center of the plant cell, the chloroplast contains large pools of diverse metabolites that can be tapped.
evidence: Stated as a property of chloroplasts

claim: Expression of genes for metabolic enzymes from the plastid genome has advantages including high expression levels, simple stacking of multiple transgenes in synthetic operons and high-precision engineering via homologous recombination.
source: Expression of genes for metabolic enzymes from the plastid genome has a number of attractions, including high expression levels, simple stacking of multiple transgenes in synthetic operons (Lu et al., 2013; Gnanasekaran et al., 2016) and high-precision engineering via homologous recombination (Maliga, 2004; Bock, 2015).
evidence: Stated as advantages with supporting citations

claim: Plastid transformation was previously employed to enhance endogenous metabolic pathways.
source: Previously, plastid transformation was employed to enhance endogenous metabolic pathways (Apel et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Plastid transformation was previously employed to produce novel metabolites, such as ketocarotenoids and biopolymers.
source: or to produce novel metabolites, such as ketocarotenoids and biopolymers (Hasunuma et al., 2008; Bohmert-Tatarev et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Two ER-resident cytochrome P450 enzymes of the dhurrin pathway were successfully expressed from a synthetic operon in tobacco chloroplasts.
source: Recently, two ER-resident cytochrome P450 enzymes of the dhurrin pathway (a cyanogenic glucoside from sorghum) were successfully expressed from a synthetic operon in tobacco chloroplasts (Gnanasekaran et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gnanasekaran et al., 2016

claim: The activity of P450 enzymes in chloroplasts was strictly light-dependent.
source: The activity of the P450 enzymes was strictly light-dependent, indicating that the electrons used come from the photosynthetic electron transport chain (Gnanasekaran et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gnanasekaran et al., 2016

claim: When P450 enzymes are anchored to the thylakoid membrane, reduced ferredoxin can replace the NADPH-dependent native reductase.
source: This suggests that, at least when P450 enzymes are anchored to the thylakoid membrane, reduced ferredoxin can replace the NADPH-dependent native reductase (Gnanasekaran et al., 2016)
evidence: Inferred from light-dependent activity, supported by citation

claim: The chloroplast is a superb compartment for the implementation of secondary metabolic pathways that involve P450-catalyzed reactions.
source: thus making the chloroplast a superb compartment for the implementation of secondary metabolic pathways that involve P450-catalyzed reactions.
evidence: Concluded from the ability of chloroplasts to support P450 enzyme activity

claim: The COSTREL approach takes advantage of the stability and high efficiency of transgene expression from the plastid genome.
source: By transplastomic introduction of the core pathway for artemisinic acid synthesis, our COSTREL approach takes advantage of the stability and high efficiency of transgene expression from the plastid genome (Maliga, 2004; Bock, 2015).
evidence: Stated as a feature of the approach with supporting citations

claim: Combinatorial supertransformation allows fine-tuning of the pathway and optimization of metabolic flux by screening metabolic phenotypes of hundreds of transgenic lines.
source: Subsequent combinatorial supertransformation of the nuclear genome with genes for auxiliary and regulatory factors then allows fine-tuning of the pathway and optimization of metabolic flux by screening metabolic phenotypes of hundreds of transgenic lines that differ in the set of transgenes they harbor in the genome and the expression levels of the transgenes (Zhu et al., 2008; Naqvi et al., 2009; 2010).
evidence: Stated as a feature of the approach with supporting citations

claim: The COSTREL approach requires no prior knowledge about the contributions of the individual factors to metabolic flux and the optimum expression strength of each transgene.
source: Importantly, this approach requires no prior knowledge about the contributions of the individual factors to metabolic flux and the optimum expression strength of each transgene.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the approach

claim: In metabolic engineering of microorganisms, success is often more dependent on achieving the optimum balance of enzyme activities than on the absolute levels of enzyme overexpression.
source: Previous metabolic engineering work in microorganisms has demonstrated that the success is often more dependent on achieving the optimum balance of enzyme activities than on the absolute levels of enzyme (over)expression (e.g., Peralta-Yahya et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peralta-Yahya et al., 2012

claim: The use of combinatorial supertransformation provides a significant advantage over the construction of large transformation vectors expressing multiple pathway genes.
source: The use of combinatorial supertransformation, therefore, provides a significant advantage over the construction of large transformation vectors expressing multiple pathway genes
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the approach

claim: The COSTREL strategy provides a new synthetic biology tool that facilitates the efficient transfer of complex metabolic pathways into new host organisms while maximizing the metabolic output.
